q: The base's confirmation e-mail reminds you to bring your papers to check-in. What goes in your hand luggage?
a: Your skipper's licence, VHF certificate, every passport and the crew list
o: Your own passport only — the base has the crew from the booking form
Your logbook and the sailing-school certificates of each crew member
The boat's registration and insurance, printed from the base's website
why: The base checks the skipper's licence and VHF certificate and files a crew list with passport numbers for the port police.

q: You fill in the crew list at the desk and the manager asks whether anyone else will sleep aboard this week. What do you say?
a: Yes — name the Wednesday guest now and tell the base again when the crew changes
o: No — a guest for two nights is not crew and does not go on the list
Yes, but you will write him on the list yourself when he arrives
No — the list is for the people who signed the charter contract
why: Everyone who sleeps aboard is on the crew list; a change mid-week is reported to the base, which amends the list for the port police.

fig.title: Crew list
lines: A friend joins Wednesday in Lefkas
Two crew fly home on Thursday
Port police may check at any harbour

q: Reading the deposit clause, your crew ask what it costs if the dinghy flips and the outboard goes to the bottom. What do you tell them?
a: The full price of the outboard — the deposit does not cap a lost dinghy or outboard
o: At most the deposit — that is exactly what the deposit is for
Nothing — the boat's insurance covers the tender and its motor
Half the price — the base shares losses that are nobody's fault
why: The deposit caps insured damage only; the contract lists what is charged in full — negligence, grounding, the dinghy and outboard.

fig.title: Contract — deposit
lines: Held on card or in cash at check-in
Limit of liability for insured damage
Dinghy and outboard: at full value

q: The desk offers you this waiver. Your crew say that with it nothing can be charged to you. What do you tell them?
a: It lowers the deposit, but the items listed as excluded are still charged in full
o: They are right — the waiver replaces the deposit and ends your liability
It covers the hull only; everything else comes off the full deposit
It is the boat's insurance; without it the base cannot let you sail
why: A waiver cuts your exposure, not the exclusions: negligence, grounding, dinghy, outboard and sails stay on the charterer.

q: The technician hands you this folder at the chart table. Where does it live during the week?
a: In the chart table, aboard, ready for a port police check in any harbour
o: At the base — the originals are too valuable to take to sea
In your bag, to show at the desk when you hand the boat back
At the marina office of your first harbour, with the crew list
why: The boat's papers sail with the boat: port police check the registration, insurance, radio licence and charter permit.

q: Your crew want to cross to Italy on Tuesday night and be back by Thursday. You read this clause. What do you do?
a: Ask the base for written consent before you leave; without it the crossing is off
o: Go, and call the base from Italy so that they know where the boat is
Go by day only — the clause forbids night sailing, not the crossing
Go — the limits bind the boat's insurer, not the skipper
why: Outside the contract area or at night the insurance and the deposit cap fall away; only the base's written consent moves a limit.

fig.title: Contract — navigation limits
lines: No sailing between sunset and sunrise

q: Your crew point at the late-return clause and say you must leave now. What do you do?
a: Stay in port, call the base now and agree with them what happens about the return
o: Leave at once with two reefs — the wind limit is advice, the penalty is money
Leave under engine only — the wind limit is about sailing, not motoring
Leave on Friday at dawn instead; one day of F7 is a smaller risk than two
why: A wind limit in the contract is a limit; the base would rather move the return than have the boat out in F7.

fig.title: Thursday 07:00, Kioni
lines: Forecast: NW 6–7 all day and Friday
Contract: no leaving port above F6

q: The manager runs through the chart briefing fast, pointing at the wall chart. What do you do with what he says?
a: Write it on your chart as he goes and ask him to repeat anything you missed
o: Listen — the pilot book covers it all and you can read it on passage
Photograph the wall chart and work out the details at sea
Note the no-go areas only; the rest is local colour
why: The chart briefing is local knowledge the pilot book lacks: hazards, no-go bays, harbours untenable in a given wind.

fig.title: Chart briefing
lines: Reef off the cape: keep 0.5 M off
Bay with the cable: no anchoring

q: The technician offers to do the technical briefing on the pontoon in five minutes, 'since you have sailed this type before'. What do you say?
a: Ask to go through each system aboard, hands on, with every switch and valve shown
o: Accept — the same model has the same systems at every base
Accept, and read the owner's manual aboard tonight instead
Accept, but ask for the briefing on paper to read on passage
why: Every charter boat is wired and plumbed differently; switches, valves and quirks are shown aboard by the one who knows them.

fig.title: Technical briefing
lines: Gas: bottle in locker, valve under sink

q: The manager ends the briefing with this slide. What do you do with it every morning of the week?
a: Check the named sources before deciding the day's passage, and call the base if in doubt
o: Check your phone's weather app — the sources listed are for the base's own use
Wait for the base to call before leaving harbour each day
Look at the sky and the barometer; forecasts are for open-sea crossings
why: The briefing names the forecasts the base trusts for its area; the daily decision to sail starts with them.

q: On Wednesday the forecast shows a gale for Friday, so you plan to be back at the base on Thursday evening. What does the contract say about that?
a: Nothing is refunded for the unused day; the berth is yours from Thursday — tell the base you are coming
o: The unused day is refunded at the daily rate
You must stay out until the return time in the contract
The deposit is reduced by one day's charter
why: Coming back early is your call and costs nothing extra; unused days are not refunded; call the base so a berth is free.

fig.title: Charter contract — return
lines: Return: Friday by 18:00, at the base
Early return: no refund of unused days
Late return: a fee per hour started

q: Your crew want to spend Friday night in a bay an hour from the base — the flights are not until Saturday noon. What do you tell them?
a: No — the boat is in the base marina on Friday evening; Saturday morning is the check-out
o: Fine — check-out is at 09:00 and an hour's sail gets you there in time
Fine, if you leave the bay at 06:00 and refuel on the way in
Fine — the base can check the boat out in the bay if you call them
why: The contract wants the boat back the evening before: the base checks her out, refuels and cleans her before the next crew.

fig.title: Contract — times
lines: Boat in base marina: Friday by 18:00
Late return: a penalty per hour, plus costs

q: The technician fills in the form as you walk round and hands it to you to sign. What do you do before you sign?
a: Read every line against what you saw, add what is missing, then photograph the form and the boat
o: Sign — the technician's copy is the one that counts and he has written it all down
Sign, and photograph the boat later in the evening when it is quieter
Sign, and e-mail the base a list of everything else you can remember
why: The check-in form is what the deposit is settled against; anything not on it counts as new damage at check-out.

q: Your partner also holds a licence and will skipper half the week. The contract looks like this. What do you do?
a: Have the base add them as co-skipper now, licence shown, before the contract is signed
o: Nothing — once the skipper is checked, anyone aboard may take the helm
Add their name to the crew list and leave the contract as it is
Carry their licence aboard and show it only if the port police ask
why: Only the skipper named in the contract is covered at the helm; a co-skipper is added at the base, with their licence, before signing.

fig.title: Charter contract — crew
lines: Crew: 6 adults on the crew list

q: At the office the desk asks you to sign the contract and the check-in form together, 'the technician will walk you round afterwards'. What do you do?
a: Sign the contract; the check-in form only after the walk-round, with what you found on it
o: Sign both — the walk-round is a formality and the form can be amended by e-mail
Sign neither until the technician has walked you round the boat
Sign both, and photograph the boat so that you have your own record
why: The check-in form records the state of the boat as you took her over; it is signed after the walk-round, not before.

q: It is 19:30 on Saturday, the base is handing over twelve boats, and the technician says 'she's fine, sign here, I'll come by tomorrow if anything is wrong'. What do you do?
a: Walk round yourself now, write what you find on the form, and have the base countersign it tonight
o: Sign — he has seen the boat, and you will phone the base about anything tomorrow
Refuse to sign, sleep ashore and come back on Sunday morning when it is quieter
Sign now, then e-mail the base a list of defects first thing on Sunday
why: The walk-round is yours, not the base's; what is not written and countersigned before you sign is yours to pay for.

q: Friday 16:00, the base is in sight and the tank is at three-quarters. Where do you take the boat first?
a: A — fill up, then berth at B and report to the base
o: B — berth; the base fills up from the berth on Saturday morning
C — the visitor quay for the night; the return berth is for Saturday
B — berth; the base's refuelling costs the same as the pontoon
why: Full to full: the boat comes back with full tanks; refuelling by the base is charged on top of the fuel.

fig.note: Fri 18:00, tanks full · base refuels at fuel + €80

q: Your crew say you can hand-haul the anchor all week and mention the windlass on Friday. What do you do?
a: Call the base now, report it, and sail on only as they instruct
o: Hand-haul for the week and write the windlass on the check-out form
Open the windlass and repair it yourselves so that nothing is charged
Sail on to the next big harbour and find a mechanic there yourselves
why: Under the contract the skipper reports a fault at once and does not carry on with it; the base decides the repair.

fig.title: Tuesday, Vathi, 12 M from base
lines: Windlass stops with 20 m of chain out
Contract: no sailing with a known fault

q: The other skipper is holding out the cash. What do you do?
a: Refuse the cash, take the boat's name, port, insurer and photos, and call the base at once
o: Take the cash — it will cover the gelcoat and the base need not know
Let him go, and have the pulpit straightened at the yard here today
Take the cash and write the damage on the check-out form on Friday
why: A third-party collision is settled between insurers: the base needs the other boat's details, photos and your report at once.

fig.title: Wednesday, Fiskardo
lines: A departing motorboat hits your bow
Their skipper offers €200 cash to settle
Base number on the chart table

q: In your first harbour the port police come aboard and ask for the boat's papers. What do you hand them?
a: The document folder: transit log, crew list, registration and insurance
o: Your skipper's licence and passport — the rest is the base's business
The charter contract — it shows that the base is responsible for the boat
A photo of the papers on your phone; the originals stay at the base
why: Port police check the transit log and crew list against the registration and insurance; they must be aboard and current.

fig.title: Port papers
lines: Transit log, stamped at the base
